framework.why: The framework provides the HTTP server integration, dependency injection, configuration and links to other libraries. In C++ terms, it's closer to a large application framework like Qt than to a small library.

options.name: Spring Boot
options.sum: The most widely used Java application framework.
pros: Easy to find documentation and help
Common skill in Java job listings
Strong first-party support for data, security and testing
cons: Usually uses more memory than compile-time frameworks
Startup is slower without native compilation
Auto-configuration can feel like hidden behavior
Many wiring errors appear at startup, not compile time
Major versions rename things, as Boot 4 did

options.name: Quarkus
options.sum: A Java framework designed for containers, fast startup and native executables, backed by Red Hat.
pros: Fast startup and low memory use
Good fit for containers and scale-to-zero hosting
cons: Smaller ecosystem than Spring
Fewer tutorials and developers
Native builds are slow and need extra setup
Some libraries need Quarkus-specific extensions
Spring skills and libraries don't carry over directly

options.name: Micronaut
options.sum: A framework that does dependency injection at compile time.
pros: Compile-time injection catches some errors earlier
Fast startup and low memory use
cons: Smaller community than Spring or Quarkus
Fewer third-party integrations
Fewer learning resources
Annotation processing adds build-time work
Harder to hire for on a team

options.name: Jakarta EE
options.sum: A vendor-neutral set of Java specifications, run on servers such as WildFly, Open Liberty or Payara.
pros: Standard APIs from a vendor-neutral foundation
Concepts carry over to Quarkus and Spring
cons: Less convenient setup than Spring Boot
Slower feature evolution
Application servers add operational weight
Fewer modern starter-style integrations
Portability can still be limited by server-specific features

build.why: The build tool compiles the code, fetches libraries, runs tests and packages the app.

options.name: Maven
options.sum: A declarative XML build with fixed lifecycle phases.
pros: Easy for tools and developers to understand
cons: XML is verbose
Custom build logic is awkward
Often slower than Gradle on larger builds
Multi-module builds can become repetitive
Less flexible when the build doesn't fit its model

options.name: Gradle
options.sum: A build tool configured with a Kotlin or Groovy script.
pros: Build cache and incremental builds can be fast
Has a wrapper that needs no admin install
cons: Steeper learning curve
Build scripts are code that can become complex
Major upgrades can break plugins or scripts
Its background daemon uses memory
Builds vary more between projects

frontend.why: This decides how users see the site. In a server-rendered site, your backend produces the HTML. In a single-page app, JavaScript or TypeScript in the browser builds the page and calls your API.

options.name: React
options.sum: A very popular JavaScript library for building interfaces from components.
pros: Very large ecosystem and job market
Frontend can be replaced without changing the backend
cons: Adds a second language and toolchain
You must choose routing and state tools
Needs a separate API and login flow
Dependency churn takes ongoing maintenance
Search visibility needs extra care for public pages

options.name: Vue
options.sum: A component framework known for its gentle learning curve and single-file components.
pros: Easier to start with than many alternatives
Can be added gradually to existing pages
cons: Smaller job market than React
Fewer third-party libraries than React
Still adds a JavaScript toolchain
Still needs an API for a full single-page app
Less common in large enterprises than Angular or React

options.name: Angular
options.sum: A complete TypeScript framework with strong conventions.
pros: Includes routing, forms and HTTP tools
cons: Largest concept count of these options
More code for small screens
Regular upgrades need attention
Heavy for a simple admin app
Needs a separate API and frontend build

options.name: Thymeleaf with htmx
options.sum: Java renders HTML templates, while htmx updates parts of a page from HTML attributes without much custom JavaScript.
pros: One app, one build and one deployment
Spring Boot has a Thymeleaf starter
Small amount of JavaScript to maintain
cons: Not ideal for very rich browser interactions
Offline behavior is difficult
Mobile apps can't reuse HTML endpoints like an API
Fewer ready-made rich components
Interaction logic can spread across templates and controllers

options.name: Vaadin
options.sum: A framework for writing web interfaces in Java components, with server-side state. Vaadin 25 supports Spring Boot 4.
pros: Write most of the interface in Java
Less need to design a separate API
cons: Server-side UI state uses memory per user
Less suited to public, content-heavy sites
Custom designs can take more effort
Stronger framework lock-in
Some tools and components may need a paid plan, so check the license

api.why: This decides how the frontend and other clients talk to the backend. If Java renders your pages, you may not need a public API at all.

options.name: Server-rendered pages
options.sum: Controllers return HTML and forms post back to the server. No public API is needed.
pros: No API contract to keep in sync
Fast to build common forms and tables
cons: Other clients can't reuse the endpoints easily
Couples the interface to the backend
Rich interactions are harder
Adding a mobile app later means adding an API
Testing HTML is less convenient than testing JSON

options.name: REST with OpenAPI
options.sum: Resources over HTTP, usually using JSON, documented by an OpenAPI description.
pros: Understood by almost every client and developer
Works with standard HTTP tools such as curl
OpenAPI can generate docs and clients
cons: Clients can receive too much or too little data
Some screens need several calls
Versioning needs a clear policy
Conventions vary without a strict design
The documentation can drift without tooling

options.name: GraphQL
options.sum: Clients send a query for exactly the fields they need.
pros: Clients request exactly the fields they need
One request can fetch related data
A typed schema documents the API
Helps when many different clients need different data
cons: More concepts than REST
Standard HTTP caching is harder
Unbounded queries need protection
The N+1 query problem needs active handling
Overkill for a simple CRUD app

options.name: gRPC
options.sum: A compact binary RPC protocol using Protocol Buffers, comparable to generated C++ client and server stubs. Boot 4.1.2 has no spring-boot-starter-grpc, so it needs a separate integration.
pros: Generates clients for many languages, including C++
cons: Browsers can't call native gRPC directly
Usually needs a proxy or gateway for web clients
Harder to inspect than JSON
Adds code generation to the build
Poor fit for a single common web app

database.why: The database holds your persistent data.

options.name: PostgreSQL
options.sum: A powerful open-source relational database.
pros: Strong SQL and data integrity features
Good JSON support alongside relational tables
Widely offered as a managed service
cons: Vacuuming and tuning need some understanding
Connection pooling matters under load
Horizontal write scaling needs extra tooling
Major version upgrades need planning
More features than a very small app may use

options.name: MySQL or MariaDB
options.sum: Very widely deployed relational databases. MariaDB began as a fork of MySQL, and they have since diverged.
cons: Fewer advanced SQL features than PostgreSQL
MySQL and MariaDB differ, so compatibility isn't guaranteed
Oracle controls MySQL's direction, and its public development has slowed
MySQL's GPL or commercial licensing can need review if you distribute it
Storage engine and configuration choices can affect behavior

options.name: SQL Server
options.sum: Microsoft's relational database, common in organizations that already use Microsoft products.
pros: Spring Boot manages the JDBC driver
cons: Paid editions can be expensive
Free Express edition has limits
Best tooling is on Microsoft platforms
Free jOOQ edition doesn't support it
Stronger vendor lock-in

options.name: MongoDB
options.sum: A document database that stores flexible, JSON-like records instead of relational tables.
cons: Relational data needs careful document design
Joins are less natural than in SQL
Flexible schemas can hide inconsistent data
Rules out JPA, jOOQ and SQL-based migrations
SSPL isn't an OSI-approved open-source license

options.name: H2
options.sum: A small Java database that runs inside your app. It's best for learning and quick experiments, not production.
pros: Can imitate some other databases' SQL
cons: In-memory data disappears on restart
Not meant for production apps
SQL differs from your eventual database
One app process owns the in-memory database
Few hosting providers offer it, because it runs inside your app

data.why: This decides how Java talks to a relational database. The tradeoff is between writing less SQL and controlling exactly what runs.

options.name: Spring Data JPA with Hibernate
options.sum: Maps objects to rows and generates common SQL.
pros: Very little code for common operations
Queries can come from method names
cons: Generated SQL can be surprising
Accidental N+1 queries are common
Lazy loading and sessions take time to understand
Complex reports fit it poorly
Entities must follow framework rules

options.name: Spring Data JDBC
options.sum: A simpler Spring Data option without lazy loading, a persistence context or automatic change tracking.
cons: Fewer relationship features
You write more custom SQL
No automatic table generation from entities
Smaller community than JPA
Aggregate design needs thought

options.name: jOOQ
options.sum: Generates Java from your schema so you can write type-checked SQL in Java, a bit like getting compiler errors for query mistakes.
pros: Compile-time checks for many query mistakes
Excellent for complex queries and reports
cons: Adds a code generation step
You must know SQL well
More code for simple CRUD
Doesn't manage object relationships like JPA
Oracle and SQL Server need a commercial edition

options.name: MyBatis
options.sum: Maps hand-written SQL, in annotations or XML, to Java objects.
pros: Good for existing or unusual schemas
cons: You write most queries yourself
Many SQL errors appear only at runtime
XML mappers can become large
Spring integration comes from the MyBatis project
Repetitive for simple CRUD

migrations.why: Migrations are versioned changes to your tables. They do for the database what Git does for source code: everyone can get from one known version to the next.

options.name: Flyway
options.sum: Runs numbered migration files, normally plain SQL, in order. Spring Boot provides spring-boot-starter-flyway.
pros: Plain SQL is easy to review
cons: Undo migrations need a paid edition
SQL is often database-specific
Applied files shouldn't be edited
Branches can create version conflicts
PostgreSQL needs an extra database module

options.name: Liquibase
options.sum: Tracks changes in XML, YAML, JSON or SQL changelogs, with more database-independent options.
pros: Can describe changes independently of the database
cons: More concepts than Flyway
Changelogs can become verbose
Version 5 uses the FSL, which isn't OSI open source
Abstractions can hide the exact SQL
Automatic rollback doesn't cover every change

login.why: Login has two parts: authentication proves who someone is, and authorization decides what they can do. Whatever you choose for authentication, your app still needs rules such as "only admins can open this page."

options.name: Spring Security with your own users
options.sum: Your app stores users and password hashes and uses server sessions.
pros: No extra service or monthly vendor bill
Full control of login pages and user data
Simple role checks with Spring Security
cons: You're responsible for stored credentials
You must build password reset flows
Multi-factor login takes extra work
Social login takes extra work
Single sign-on across apps isn't included

options.name: Keycloak
options.sum: An open-source identity server you run yourself. Your app signs users in through OpenID Connect. It runs from a ZIP on a supported JDK.
pros: Open source with no per-user fee
Has its own user administration console
Keeps user data on infrastructure you control
cons: One more service to run and secure
Needs its own production database
You handle upgrades and backups
Many concepts for a small app
Theme customization takes effort

options.name: Auth0
options.sum: A hosted identity service. Its pricing page lists a free plan of up to 25,000 monthly active users, with limits on features.
pros: Multi-factor and social login are available
Free tier can cover a small project
cons: Costs can rise with users and features
Harder to migrate away from later
Outages can stop people logging in
User data sits with a third party
Plans and limits can change

options.name: Microsoft Entra External ID
options.sum: Microsoft's hosted customer identity service. Its core offering is free for the first 50,000 monthly active users, while premium add-ons cost extra.
cons: Tied to Microsoft's cloud
Portal and concepts can feel complex
Some security features are paid add-ons
Fewer independent tutorials than Auth0 or Keycloak
Harder to migrate away from later

admin.why: This is the area where trusted staff manage users and business data. Whichever option you choose, enforce admin permissions on the server, not only in the interface.

options.name: Pages in your app
options.sum: Build admin screens with the same frontend as the rest of the app, under a path such as /admin.
pros: Full control over screens and workflows
Reuses your login, roles and business logic
Good practice for learning your framework
cons: You build every screen
Tables, filters and exports take time
Admin bugs can affect the main app
Shared deployment means a shared release cycle
Needs its own tests and audit logging

options.name: React-admin
options.sum: A React framework for building admin interfaces on top of an API.
pros: Much faster than building each screen
Can connect to your own REST API
Keeps business logic behind your API
cons: Requires React and JavaScript skills
Requires a well-designed API
Adds a separate frontend build
Customization outside its patterns can be hard
Some advanced modules are paid

options.name: Vaadin admin views
options.sum: Build admin screens in Java with data grids and forms, even if the public site uses something else.
pros: Can call your Spring services directly
Few admin users limits its memory concern
cons: Adds a substantial dependency
Different interface model from the rest of the app
Some features may need a paid plan
Upgrades can require code changes
Ties your admin area to one vendor's framework

options.name: Retool or Appsmith
options.sum: Low-code tools for assembling internal interfaces from databases and APIs.
pros: Very fast to create internal tools
cons: Direct database access can bypass business rules
Extra platform to pay for or host
Harder to version and test like normal code
Vendor lock-in
Teaches you little about your framework

hosting.why: This decides where the app and database run in production. Cost and limits vary by provider, so compare current pricing before you write the ADR.

options.name: Platform as a service
options.sum: Services such as Render, Railway or Fly.io build and run your app from your Git repository or container image.
pros: Handles servers and HTTPS for you
cons: Usually costs more per resource at scale
Less control over the environment
Provider limits can affect your design
Migration takes work if you outgrow it
Data region options may be limited

options.name: Managed containers
options.sum: Services such as Azure Container Apps, AWS ECS or Google Cloud Run run your container without you managing Kubernetes.
pros: Scales well beyond a small app
Integrates with cloud networking and identity
Managed databases sit in the same cloud
cons: Cloud permissions and networking are complex
Bills can be hard to predict
More setup than a platform service
Cloud-specific configuration causes lock-in
Slow JVM startup can matter when scaling from zero

options.name: A virtual private server
options.sum: Rent one Linux server and run your jar or Docker Compose yourself.
pros: Great way to learn Linux and networking
cons: You handle security patches
You handle backups and monitoring
One server is a single point of failure
Scaling is largely manual
Mistakes can expose the app or its data

options.name: Kubernetes
options.sum: A system for running many containers across many machines, usually through a managed service.
pros: Suits many services and large teams
cons: Far too complex for one small web app
Ongoing operational work and upgrades
Cluster costs add up
Security configuration is easy to get wrong
Local setup adds another tool to learn
